name: jasmin
desc: Assembler for the Java Virtual Machine
why: Writing JVM bytecode by hand exposes the machine beneath Java, a strange and instructive way to see how programs really run.

brief.what_it_is: Jasmin is an assembler for the Java Virtual Machine. It takes ASCII source files written in a simple assembler-like syntax that uses JVM instruction mnemonics, and converts them into binary Java .class files that a Java runtime can load. The source file's .class directive decides where the output class file goes. The assembler does little checking: it does not verify that referenced classes exist or that type descriptors are well formed.
brief.why_it_exists: Jasmin was created by Jon Meyer as a companion to his O'Reilly book 'Java Virtual Machine', so readers could try out JVM features directly. The homepage says it has since become the de-facto standard assembly format for Java and is used in dozens of compiler classes around the world.
brief.how_it_works: Source is tokenized on whitespace into directives (names starting with '.'), instructions (standard JVM opcode mnemonics), and labels. Class and method names use class-file conventions, so java/lang/String rather than java.lang.String, and methods are written as one token such as java/io/PrintStream/println(Ljava/lang/String;)V. The assembler emits a class file; with -g it adds line-number information for debuggers.

brief.install_notes: Download is from SourceForge; the homepage gives no other install steps. Running requires a Java runtime, invoked as java -jar jasmin.jar or java Jasmin with the jar on the classpath. The guide says nothing about configuration or accounts. No Homebrew-specific notes were in the brew data.
brief.standout: Jasmin is a thin, literal assembler: it maps almost one-to-one onto class-file structure and deliberately skips verification, so you can hand-write bytecode that a compiler would never emit and see what the JVM does with it. The guide is candid that it is a teaching and experimentation tool, not a macro assembler.
brief.status: Quiet by the evidence available. The homepage was last dated Dec 2005 (Daniel Reynaud), the user guide is dated July 1996, and the page mentions version 2.1 enhancements and JasminXT since 2.0. I saw no release date or commit history, so I cannot confirm recent maintenance.
brief.caveats: The assembler does no compile-time checking of class references or descriptors, so mistakes show up only at runtime or in the verifier. Numeric support is limited: no scientific notation, character literals, or octal. String escape support is basic, with only \n and \t documented. Labels cannot start with a digit or contain = : . " -. Methods get no implicit return and must end with one. The guide doesn't cover every instruction; the JVM spec is needed for that. The homepage's 'Download' link to SourceForge was not followed, so I have no version number or licence statement. The homepage's copyright line is 2004, Jonathan Meyer.
